To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the unfolding changes in preferentially bound water (ΔΓ21), as determined by membrane-free osmometry, are smaller than expected on the basis of theoretical models, and that the discrepancy is not the result of a strong cosolvent–protein interaction.

the cosolvent concentration dependence of the unfolding ΔH and ΔCp is very small; the unfolding ΔΓ21 is smaller than ΔN1; the ΔΓ21 value is sensitive to the protein–cosolvents interaction; and the ΔΓ21 data are compatible with the two-domain (bulk–local) solvent model.

the unfolding enthalpies of two proteins are independent of cosolvent concentration; the unfolding heat capacities of two proteins are only marginally affected by cosolvent concentration (the effect is not significant); the unfolding changes in preferentially bound cosolvent are smaller than expected from the number of water monolayers removed from the protein surface; the two-domain (bulk-local) solvent model can explain the experimental findings.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effect of preferential hydration changes on the energetics of protein conformational transitions and, in particular, with the question of how the cosolvent-induced changes in preferential solvent interaction may affect the thermodynamics of the unfolding transition.

the analysis of the thermodynamics of protein unfolding as a function of cosolvent concentration, and it is aimed at understanding the effect of cosolvents on the protein hydration changes upon unfolding.
the analysis of the thermodynamic properties of protein–cosolvents interactions, and the effect of these interactions on protein stability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ΔΓ21 data are not sufficient by themselves for a quantitative characterization of the cosolvent effect on the protein unfolding process, and a detailed thermodynamic characterization is needed.

the cosolvent concentration dependence of the unfolding enthalpies and heat capacities is not significant in this work, but that the unfolding changes in hydration are significantly smaller than expected.

the ΔΓ21 value for the unfolding of ribonucleanse a and hen egg lysozyme in the presence of cosolvents is smaller than the ΔN1 value because the local domain of both the native and unfolded protein is not completely devoid of cosolvent molecules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the systems studied, the ΔΓ values are not a good indicator of the ΔN values, and that the latter should be estimated from other, more reliable, experimental data.

the cosolvent effect on the protein unfolding energetics is small and the corresponding ΔΓ21 values, although significantly different from ΔN1, are still in good agreement with the theoretical estimates of the number (N2) of water molecules corresponding first to the second and then to the third layer of solvent molecules in the protein surface.

the hydration changes upon protein unfolding are significantly smaller than those predicted by the local-bulk model, and that this is the case for a wide variety of cosolvents, including those expected to be excluded from the native protein surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in order to obtain a reliable estimate of the number of hydration water molecules involved in a protein unfolding transition, one needs to take into account the effect of the cosolvent in both the bulk and the protein local domains.

, when the ΔΓ21 data are used for the analysis of protein conformational equilibria in the presence of cosolvents, the ΔΓ values should be corrected for the cosolvent concentration, and the ΔΓ21–ΔΓ relationship should be calibrated by comparison with the ΔN1 values calculated from a suitable model of the protein structure in solution.

, in order to correctly estimate the number of water molecule involved in protein confectional changes, one should not use the membrane-free ΔΓ21 values, but rather the ΔN1 values calculated on the basis of the two-domain model.
